Transpire is a verb with more than one meaning, and understanding all of them — plus an important controversy around the word — is the key to fully mastering it.

This is the original, formal meaning of the word, and the one that careful writers prefer.

When something transpires, it means that information which was previously secret, hidden, or unknown comes to light — it becomes known to people.

Think of it like a secret leaking out into the open.

Examples:

  • "It transpired that the company had been hiding its losses for years."
    → It came to light / became known that the company had been hiding its losses.
  • "It later transpired that no one had actually seen the accident happen."
    → It later became clear that no one had witnessed it.
  • "What transpired behind closed doors eventually reached the media."
    → What was said and done in private eventually became public.

Notice the pattern: you'll very often see "it transpired that...", which is a classic, reliable way to use the word in this sense. The "it" is a placeholder, and the real information comes after "that."
Meaning 2: To Happen or Occur (Common but Controversial)

Over time, many people started using transpire simply to mean "to happen" or "to take place." This usage is now extremely common — you'll encounter it everywhere.

Examples:

  • "Tell me everything that transpired at the meeting."
    → Tell me everything that happened at the meeting.
  • "The events that transpired last night were shocking."
    → The events that occurred last night were shocking.
  • "No one knows exactly what transpired between them."
    → No one knows exactly what happened between them.

⚠️ The Controversy You Should Know About

This second meaning is disputed. Many grammar experts, editors, and style guides strongly object to it. Their argument is straightforward: the word already has a precise meaning (to become known), so using it loosely to mean "to happen" is a waste of a useful word — like using a scalpel as a butter knife.

Here's the problem in action:

"It transpired that they argued."

Using Meaning 1: It came to light that they argued. ✅
Using Meaning 2: It happened that they argued. ✅

Both readings are technically possible, which creates ambiguity — something good writing always avoids.

The practical advice: In formal writing (essays, reports, professional emails), stick to Meaning 1 — to become known. It is more precise, more impressive, and never wrong. In casual speech and informal writing, using it to mean "to happen" is widely understood and accepted, though some readers may notice.
Meaning 3: In Science — Plants Releasing Water Vapor

In biology and botany, transpire has a distinct, technical meaning: it refers to the process by which plants release water vapor from their leaves into the air, through tiny pores called stomata.

Think of it as a plant "breathing out" moisture.

Examples:

  • "Plants transpire more rapidly in hot, dry conditions."
  • "A single large tree can transpire hundreds of liters of water per day."

This process is called transpiration, and it plays a major role in the water cycle — the moisture plants release into the air eventually becomes clouds and rain.

While this meaning is less likely to come up in everyday conversation, it's important to know, especially for science contexts.

Here is a simple way to remember the three meanings:

  • In formal/general language: transpire = something hidden comes to light (becomes known). ← The "best" usage.
  • In common usage: transpire = to happen or take place. ← Widely used but disputed.
  • In science: transpire = a plant releases water vapor through its leaves.

The most powerful version of this word — the one that will make your writing look sharp and precise — is the first one. When you write "it transpired that...", you are using the word exactly as it was meant to be used, and it carries a quiet elegance that "it turned out that" simply does not.
